title: Claude Haiku 5.5 Launches at $0.10 per Million Input Tokens
subtitle: Anthropic's new small model is roughly 75% cheaper than Haiku 4.5 and adds configurable effort levels for high-volume work.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic released Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7, 2026, completing its Claude 5.5 family after earlier Opus and Sonnet updates. The small model is available on the Anthropic API, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex, and Microsoft Azure under the identifier claude-haiku-5-5. Below 100,000 tokens, input costs $0.10 per million and output costs $0.50 per million — a drop of roughly 75% from Haiku 4.5's $1 and $5 rates. Above that threshold, the rates rise to $0.50 and $2.50. The release also adds configurable effort levels, letting developers trade token spend for capability on a per-task basis.

The pricing change — not the capability jump — is the story. On vendor-reported benchmarks like the offline subset of OSWorld 2.1 for computer use, Haiku 5.5 scores 72.4% versus 15.7% for Haiku 4.5, which is a large gain but one that still needs independent testing. What matters commercially is the per-token cost falling into a range where high-volume agent workloads become economic. Agents that run thousands of tool calls per task, batch classifiers, and background summarizers all become cheaper to deploy by about four times without a model swap.

The 5.5 family now covers the full spectrum. Opus handles long-horizon reasoning, Sonnet is the mid-tier default released on October 6, and Haiku takes the floor for fast, cheap calls or as a subagent coordinated by Opus or Sonnet. That shape mirrors how Anthropic's enterprise customers already deploy Claude — a planner model orchestrating cheaper worker models — and the Haiku price cut makes that pattern more affordable to scale. OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol release the previous week pushed on the same cost-performance curve, suggesting the frontier labs are competing as much on inference economics as on headline capability.

A note for learners: when a lab cuts small-model prices this sharply, it is usually a signal that the economics of running inference at that tier have improved — through better model distillation, cheaper hardware, or new serving tricks — not just a marketing move. Watch for which workloads shift from the mid-tier down to the small tier over the next quarter. That migration is where the real cost savings land for teams building on top of these APIs.
